en: Prosperity! Now, on Phonetics (Śikṣā). Now I shall proclaim the phonetics according to the doctrine of Pāṇini; one should know that sequence of the treatise as it has been stated for both the worldly and Vedic languages. (1) Although the meaning of words is well-known, it remains uncomprehended by those lacking intelligence; therefore, I shall again clarify the rule for the pronunciation of speech. (2) Sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes are recognized in the tradition of Śambhu; they were proclaimed by the Self-Existent One himself for both Prakrit and Saṃskṛta. (3)

There are twenty-one vowels and twenty-five consonants; the letters from *ya* onwards are recorded as eight, and the *yamas* are recorded as four. The *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, and those dependent on the following letter, as well as the *duḥspṛṣṭa* and the *ḷ*-vowel which is indeed extraordinary, are to be known [as such]. The self (*ātman*), through the intellect (*buddhi*), perceives objects with the mind (*manas*) when there is a desire to speak. The mind strikes the fire of the body (*kāyāgni*), and that fire impels the vital air (*māruta*). Moving within the chest, the vital air produces the deep-toned (*mandra*) sound.

O Mother, that wind which is joined with the morning libation (*savana*) and rests upon the *gāyatrī* meter; which, reaching the throat, is joined with the midday libation and the middle *triṣṭubh* meter; and which, rising to the head, is joined with the third (*tārtīya*) libation and the *jagatī* meter—this wind, when it is exhaled and struck at the head, reaches the palate and produces the phonemes (*varṇas*). Their classification is recorded as fivefold: by accent (*svara*), by duration (*kāla*), by place of articulation (*sthāna*), by internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*), and by external effort (*bāhya-pratyāpādāna*). Thus say those who know the phonemes; understand this thoroughly.

10 || 2 || There are three accents: acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), and circumflex (svarita). Short, long, and protracted—these are the restrictions regarding duration when followed by a vowel (ac). || 11 || In the acute accent lie Niṣāda and Gāndhāra; in the grave, Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata. These six—Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Pañcama—originate from the circumflex. || 12 || There are eight places of articulation for the phonemes (varṇas): the chest, the throat, and likewise the head; the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate. || 13 ||

Luminosity (*obhāva*), openness (*vivṛtti*), *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *r*, as well as the root of the tongue (*jihvāmūla*) and the labio-dental (*upadhmāna*), are the eightfold movement of the spirants (*ūṣman*). (14) If there is a word beginning with *u* and so forth that lacks conjunction (*asaṃdhāna*) and possesses luminosity, one should know such a word to end in a vowel; anything else is clearly a spirant. (15) One should know the letter *ha* when joined with the fifth [consonants] or with the semivowels (*antasthā*) to be guttural (*aurasya*); they say it is guttural when unjoined. The retroflex sounds *ṛ*, *ṭu*, and *ra* are known as cerebrals (*mūrdhanya*); the dentals *tu*, *la*, and *sa* are remembered as dentals (*dantya*). The sound *ku* is said to be produced at the root of the tongue, while *va* is recorded by the wise as a dental-labial (*dantyoṣṭhya*). The vowels *ai* and *ai* are palatal (*kaṇṭhatālavya*), while *au* and *au* are recorded as labiovelar (*kaṇṭhoṣṭha*). The half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) belongs to the velar (*kaṇṭhya*) position in the case of *e* and *o*. The mora (*mātrā*) for *ai* and *au* consists of both the open (*vivṛta*) and the closed (*saṃvṛta*) articulations. The closed articulation should be known as having one mora (*mātrika*), whereas the open articulation has two moras (*dvimātrika*).

All voiced consonants are considered closed (saṃvṛta), while unvoiced ones are known to be open (vivṛta). The articulation of the vowels and the sibilants (ūṣman) is traditionally held to be open; among those, e and o are more open than the others, and ai and au are even more so. The nose is said to be the place of articulation for the anusvāra and the *yamas*. The *ayogavāhas* should be understood as sharing the same points of articulation as their respective supports. Following the sounds of the gourd-lute (*alābu-vīṇā*), the nasalization (*anusvāra*) should always be applied after dental and labial vowels before the letters ś, ṣ, and s, as well as before *c* and *ch*.

One should separate the lips twice for the anusvāra, the vivṛti, the virāma, and for the pair of syllables where there is the letter *ya* and the letter *va*. (24) Just as a tigress might carry off her cubs with her fangs without causing them pain—being afraid of dropping or breaking them—one should employ the phonemes in that same manner. (25) Just as one speaks from Saurāṣṭra, so too is the instruction: the *raṅga* sounds should be employed in the *kha* [consonants] with a sense of weariness, as if in the sky. (26)

One who employs the *raṅga-varṇa* should first utter the initial syllable; one should then employ a long vowel and subsequently perform the nasalization (*nāsikya*). (27) In the heart [of the chest] it has one measure (*mātrā*), in the head half a measure, and likewise in the nose half a measure; thus the *raṅga* itself possesses two measures. (28) Standing with the body raised from the heart, sounding it with a bronze-like resonance, one attains softness and the two measures—as in the example: *jaghanvān*. (29)

In the middle, one should cause the *kampa* (vibratory movement) to shake; both sides should be equal. One should cause the *saraṅga-kampa* (the trembling with resonance) to vibrate, as the chariot provides the illustration. (30) Thus the phonemes (*varṇas*) should be employed—neither indistinct nor suppressed. By the correct application of the phonemes, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. (31) The singer, the hurried reader, the one who shakes his head, the one who reads from a written text, the one who knows only the meaning, and the one with a weak voice—these six are the lowest of reciters. (32)

Sweetness, clarity, distinct separation of words, a melodious tone, composure, and mastery over tempo—these six are the qualities of a reciter. (339) That which is marked by stress, frightened, shouted, indistinct, nasalized, like the voice of a crow, affected by rasiness, as well as devoid of proper placement; (340) whispered, bitten [by the teeth], hurried, rejected, too slow, faltering, or sung; crushed, with words and syllables swallowed, lacking in luster, or accompanied by nasality—[such recitation is faulty]. (341)

One should always recite in the morning with a sound residing in the chest, resembling the roar of a tiger; at midday, with a sound residing in the throat, similar to the cry of a ruddy goose (cakravāka). One should know that the third *savana* is high-pitched; it should always be employed with a sound residing in the head, equal to the notes of a peacock, a swan, or a cuckoo. The vowels (*ac*) are unaspirated (*aspṛṣṭā*); the semi-vowels (*yaṇ*) are slightly closed (*īṣatspṛṣṭā*); and the sibilants (*śara*) are remembered as being fully closed (*spṛṣṭā*).

The remaining consonants (hal) are said to be "contacted" (spṛṣṭa); learn them according to their degrees of openness (anunāsikatva). The *yama*s are nasalized; *ha* and *jhaṣa* are known as sonorous (*nādin*). The *yaṇ*s and *jaś*s have slight sonority, while *kha*, *pha*, and the others are aspirated (*śvāsin*). One should know that the semivowels (*cara*) have slight aspiration; this is what they declare regarding the *goṣāma*. By Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī, this [grammar] has been spread throughout the earth. Chandas is the feet of the Veda, and Kalpa is said to be its hands; Jyotiṣāmayana is its eye, and Nirukta is called its ear.

41 || Śikṣā is indeed the nose of the Veda, while Grammar is remembered as its mouth; therefore, one who knows the meaning correctly is glorified in the world of Brahman. 42 || 43 || One should know that the acute (udātta) accent is indicated by the forefinger (pradeśinī), placed with the head resting at the base of the finger; the circumflex (svarita) is held between the middle and the edge [of the fingers], and the grave (anudātta) is on the little finger (kaniṣṭhikā). 44 || One should know the acute (udātta) to be on the forefinger, the protracted (pracaya) on the middle finger, the depressed (nihata) on the little finger, and the circumflex (svarita) on the ring finger (upakaniṣṭhikā).

The nine types of word-accentuation are: oxytone (antodātta), proparoxytone (ādyudātta), acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), low-pitched circumflex (nīcasvarita), middle-acute (madhyodātta), circumflex (svarita), acute (udātta), and triple-acute (tryudātta). Regarding the verses *aṅghriḥ*, *somaḥ*, *pra vo vīryaṃ*, *haviṣāṃ*, *svaḥ*, *bṛhaspatiḥ*, *indrāvṛhaspatī*, and *agniḥ*: *aṅghriḥ* is oxytone; *somaḥ* is proparoxytone; *me* is acute; *vaḥ* is grave; and *vīryaṃ* is low-pitched circumflex. In *haviṣāṃ*, the accent is middle-acute; *saḥ* is circumflex.

“Vṛhaspati” has two udātta [accents]; “indrāvṛhaspatī” has three udātta [accents]. ||47|| The anudātta is to be known as being in the heart; the udātta is declared to be in the head; the svarita is at the root of the ear; the pracaya is remembered as being throughout the entire mouth. ||48|| The blue jay utters a single mora, while the crow utters two moras; the peacock cries out for three moras, while the mongoose [utters] half a mora. ||49|| [That which is] come from a false source, burnt, discolored, and eaten—[is not to be accepted].

For him, there is no liberation through recitation, just as one is not freed from the sin of a wicked serpent. (50) The Veda shines when it has come from a sacred place, is clearly articulated, well-established in its own tradition, and is joined with a beautiful voice and excellent syllables. (51) A mantra deficient in accent or syllable, or wrongly applied, destroys the man who utters it; like the thunderbolt of speech, it slays the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [Vṛtra] was slain due to a fault in the accentual instruction (*svaralakṣaṇa*). (52) A syllable omitted shortens one’s lifespan, while a misplaced accent afflicts one with disease.

The thunderbolt falls upon the head of one who studies [the Veda] without the hand-gesture, in the form of unbroken [syllables], and devoid of accents and phonemes. Consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [Vedas], he goes to a low birth. But he who studies the Veda with the hand-gesture, endowed with accents, phonemes, and meaning, purified by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [Vedas], is glorified in the world of Brahmā. Śaṅkara took the Śāṅkarī [Vidyā] from the son of Dakṣa, the wise one, having extracted it from all forms of speech; such is the established tradition regarding the Goddess of Speech.

Salutations to that Pāṇini, who, having received the collection of phonemes from Maheśvara, proclaimed the entire science of grammar. Salutations to that Pāṇini, by whom the speech of men was purified with the stainless waters of words, and by whom the darkness born of ignorance was shattered. Salutations to that Pāṇini, by whom the eye of the world, blinded by ignorance, was opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge.

The twice-born who, being ever disciplined, recites here this [hymn] issued from the mouth of the Three-eyed Lord, becomes possessed of wealth, grain, cattle, sons, and fame, and attains incomparable happiness in heaven after heaven. (60) 11. Now, the Śikṣā concerning the self: "The letter *ha* among the vowels is acute (*udātta*) according to the chant; it is unaspirated (*aspṛṣṭa*), and the blue jay (*cāṣa*) is the eleventh, O Śaṅkara. Thus ends the Śikṣā. Prosperity! Now follows the recitation of the Paribhāṣās.

The specific application [of a rule] is understood through its explanation; for there can be no lack of definition due to doubt. The technical names (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) follow the order in which they are enunciated. The technical names and rules of interpretation apply at the time the grammatical operation takes place. The indicatory letters (*anubandha*) are not uniform. A grammatical element does not become "having more than one letter" (*anekāl*) merely because of its indicatory letters. A grammatical element does not become "ending in a non-consonant" (*anejant*) merely because of its indicatory letters. A grammatical element does not become "dissimilar" (*asārūpya*) merely because of its indicatory letters. In this system, both ways of understanding apply. For when a grammatical element undergoes an operation, it is not treated as a cause for that very operation.

When [grammatical elements] have become a group (*gaṇa*), they are included by the mention of that group. Substitutes apply to that which is being specifically pointed out (*nirdiśyamāna*). Where there is a conflict between multiple types of proximity (*āntarya*), proximity of position (*sthāna*) is stronger. When there is the mention of a meaningful element, there is no inclusion of that which is meaningless. Between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), the operation is understood to apply to the primary. The mentions of *an*, *in*, *as*, and *man* cause the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) to apply both to meaningful and meaningless elements. For those mentioned in a single grammatical rule (*eka-yoga*), there is either simultaneous application or simultaneous cessation.

When elements are prescribed as being in a single grammatical connection (*ekayoga*), sometimes even a single portion of that connection is carried over. There is no inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) by that which is itself being taught (*bhāvyamāna*). However, the vowel *u* (in *ū*), even while being taught, does include its homogeneous sounds. When a rule depends on a specific phoneme (*varṇāśraya*), there is no application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle (which treats a form as ending in a suffix). The *uṇādi* suffixes are underived nominal stems (*avyutpannaprātipadika*). When a suffix is mentioned [in a rule], it denotes that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed and ends with the suffix itself. Furthermore, when a suffix is mentioned, it includes everything up to the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*).

In the section concerning subsequent members (*uttarapadādhikāra*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it (*tadantagrahaṇa*). Furthermore, this does not apply to feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) when they are not subordinate (*anupasarjana*). In the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it. When a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, there is inclusion of what is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. Under the headings of "word" (*pada*) and "stem" (*aṅga*), there is inclusion of both the base itself and that which ends with it. Because the cause [of the designation] exists in a single entity, it is treated as if it possessed a distinct designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). There is no inclusion of that which ends with it when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned along with a suffix. The treatment as if possessing a distinct designation does not apply to a nominal stem.

In a compound where the first member is a word ending in *vi*, there is elision of the final vowel of that first member. Every *dvandva* compound optionally becomes a singular (*ekavadbhāva*). All grammatical rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*). An imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is treated like its original form (*prakṛti*). That which is modified by the substitution of one part is not considered different from the original. Among preceding, subsequent, permanent, internal, and exceptional rules, each succeeding one is stronger than the preceding. A rule is established through the recognition of its reappearance (*punaḥprasaṅga*). When two rules apply simultaneously and are in conflict, that which is assigned priority remains assigned. A restrictive rule (*niyama*) is stronger than an affix (*vikaraṇa*).

That which is obtained by another [rule] is always stronger. A rule that applies after another word has been introduced is non-eternal (*anitya*). There is non-eternality in a rule that applies when another word has been introduced, and also in one that applies when another word has not been introduced. A rule that applies by means of another defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is non-eternal. In some cases, eternality exists even merely through the fact that an operation has already occurred or not yet occurred. That whose cause is obstructed by another defining characteristic is not non-eternal; however, that whose cause is obstructed by another defining characteristic is also non-eternal.

The rule concerning *svarabhakti* (the svarabhinnasya) is not eternal (*anitya*). That which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is considered unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*). When there is immediate proximity of vowels (*ajānantarya*), there is no consideration of what is external. The elision (*luk*), being external, subverts even internal rules. The single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not take effect before the operation conditioned by both the preceding and following words, even though it is internal. The suffixal substitute *lyap* subverts even internal rules. An internal rule (*āṅga*) is stronger than one based on phonemes (*vārṇa*). The followers of Pāṇini do not apply a rule when its conditions have already been destroyed (*akṛtavyūhāḥ*). An exception (*apavāda*) is stronger than that which is internal.

A rule that is introduced when another has not yet been applied becomes a sublater of that [prior rule]. This is the reading of the *paribhāṣā*: "An universal rule (*utsarga*) applies even in the domain of an exception (*apavāda*). Exceptions located earlier sublate the immediately following rules, but not those that follow later. Exceptions located in the middle sublate the preceding rules, but not those that follow later. "Either a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately adjacent. For exceptions take effect first, and universal rules afterwards.

The domain of the exception (*apavāda*) must first be determined, and only thereafter does the general rule (*utsarga*) take effect. Even an exception whose cause is yet to arise subverts a general rule whose cause has already arisen. If an exception finds its scope elsewhere, it is then subverted by that which is more internal (*antaraṅga*). There is no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) among repeated grammatical operations (*abhyāsavikāra*). The rule regarding non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply to suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*). Furthermore, the rule regarding non-identity of form does not apply to the suffixes *talyuṭ*, *tumun*, *khal*, and *ar*.

The rule of *vā-asarūpa* (the optionality of non-homogeneous forms) does not apply regarding substitutes (*lādeśa*). When both [the fifth and sixth case endings] are specified, the specification by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is more powerful. When a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included. In the context of case-endings (*vibhakti*), that which is qualified by gender is not included. In a sūtra, gender and number are not restrictive. When joined with *nañ* or *iva*, the reference is to something else similar; for it is in this way that the meaning is understood. There is an injunction for the compounding of prepositions (*gati*), verbal roots (*kāraka*), and secondary words (*upapada*) with primary derivatives (*kṛt*) prior to the arising of case-endings. In the absence of a contemporary [entity], there is recourse to what previously existed.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is also the "cognition of its qualities" (*taguṇasaṃvijñāna*). That which is drawn forward (*anukṛṣṭa*) does not apply to what follows. In a rule prescribing a vowel (*svaravidhi*), a consonant (*vyañjana*) is as if non-existent. A consonant is as if non-existent when a short vowel is to be obtained. When there is a mention of a form without an *anubandha*, there is no inclusion of a form with an *anubandha*. When there is a mention of a form with a specific *anubandha*, there is no inclusion of a form with a different *anubandha*. Sometimes, secondary suffixes (*svārthika*) deviate from the gender and number of the base. The rule for compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) is not universal.

A rule characterized by the combination [of two causes] is not a cause for the destruction of that [combination]. When those taught as being enjoined together (saṃniyogaśiṣṭa), upon the removal of one, there is the removal of both. In the case of a suffix characterized by the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*), the operations caused by the *aṇ* suffix apply. An operation stated for a verbal root (*dhātu*) applies to its suffix. That which falls between [two elements] is included by the mention of those [two]. Between a suffix with the augment *chuk* and a suffix without the augment *luk*, the rule applies to the one without *luk*. When a base (*prakṛti*) is mentioned, that which has an additional *ṇi* suffix is also included. There is no application of a rule when an operation has already occurred within the formation of a stem (*aṅga*).

A rule conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not invariably obligatory. A grammatical instruction (*āgamaśāstra*) is not invariably obligatory. An operation based on a *gaṇa*-list is not invariably obligatory. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*), characterized by the presence of an *anudātta* accent, is not invariably obligatory. A rule containing the negative particle *nañ* is not invariably obligatory. A rule based on extension (*ātideśika*) is not invariably obligatory. The rule for elision (*lopa*) and the rule for substitution (*vidhi*) are stronger than all other rules. When a base (*prakṛti*) is mentioned, that which ends in *yaṅ-luk* is also included. A *paribhāṣā* (technical maxim) applies to a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*), but not to a restatement (*anuvāda*). The case-ending expressing the relation of the word governed (*upapada*) is stronger than the case-ending expressing the kāraka.

In the case of a modification of the final [element], it applies to that which occupies the position immediately preceding the final. When an element is meaningless, the rule regarding the final letter does not apply, except in the case of the augment *an*. Between the principal and the subordinate, the operation is understood to apply to the principal. The conventional meaning of a whole is stronger than the etymological meaning of its parts. Grammatical operations are also performed by means of fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). When both a general injunction and a restrictive rule are possible, the injunction alone is the logical course. In the case of an extension of a general property, there is no extension of specific properties. Between a suffix and a non-suffix, only the suffix is to be understood.

Between that which is accompanied by a co-occurring element and that which is not, only that which is accompanied by a co-occurring element is to be understood. Between what is directly stated in scripture and what is inferred, the direct scriptural statement is more powerful. Between that which is indicated by definition and that which is explicitly stated in the rule, only the explicitly stated is to be understood. In rules involving the mention of *gā* and *ādi*, there is no distinction [between the general and the specific]. A sentence is completed with each individual word. Sometimes it is completed even with a collective group. Qualities do not cause differentiation. Exceptions are indeed sublaters. A grammatical rule operates like a rain-cloud. A rule applies only once to a given linguistic form (*lakṣya*).

The prohibitions and the *paribhāṣā*-readings are more powerful [than general rules]. Unspecified suffixes [denote] their own meaning (*svārtha*). Desired results are achieved through the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) and other means. Among synonymous terms, consideration for brevity (*lāghava*) or prolixity (*gaurava*) is not observed. That which is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*) does not apply everywhere. In the rule regarding what is "not established" (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it, this does not apply in the case of doubling (*aditve*). From one application of a form, there will be no application of a second or third instance of that same class (*ākṛti*). In the case of *saṃprasāraṇa* and the operation dependent upon it, the latter is stronger.

In some cases, a derivative form (*vikṛti*) takes the place of its base form (*prakṛti*). Between that which is taught directly (*aupadeśika*) and that which is derived through grammatical operations (*āyogika*), the direct teaching alone is accepted. That which is specified by *śtip*, by *śap*, by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), or by a class-name (*gaṇa*); that where there is a mention of all three times (past, present, and future); and that which does not occur in the *yaṅ* or *ślu* formations—these [are the exceptions]. A division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) is more burdensome than the weight of a word; for grammarians consider the gain of even half a mora to be a festival for their sons. Thus ends the recitation of the Paribhāṣās. May it be auspicious! Śrī!

It is optional after *yam* in the sense of "marrying" (*upayamana*). After the roots *sthā* and *pā*, the augment *iṭ* is added before *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. The augment *iṭ* is not added after the roots *śī*, *jū*, *svid*, *mid*, *kṣvid*, *dhṛṣ*, and *mṛṣ* when used in the sense of "endurance" (*titikṣā*). After a root ending in *u* as its penultimate letter, the augment is optional when the action refers to the agent or the object. After the root *pū*, both *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* take the augment optionally. After a root ending in *tha* or *pha* with a non-penultimate vowel, the augment is optional. This is the reading of the Sūtra-text: Aṣṭādhyāyī, Pāda 1, Adhyāya 2, Sūtras 1–2. Furthermore, the *vaṣaṭ* call may be uttered at a higher pitch, or it is optional in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).

In the *subrahmaṇyā* formula, [the vowel] that was circumflex (*svarita*) becomes acute (*udātta*). In the words *deva* and *brahman*, [the vowel] becomes grave (*anudātta*). In a *saṃhitā* (continuous text), following a circumflex vowel, the grave vowels [become circumflex]. [The word] *vrataraḥ* [is an exception]. A single phoneme (*ekāl*) suffix that follows an acute or circumflex vowel [becomes circumflex]. A *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members refer to the same object is called *karmadhāraya*. In a compound, that which is designated by the first case [retains its original accent].

When the sense [of the agent] is understood through a governing word (*vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne*), the *parasmaipada* suffixes are used for the remaining roots in the sense of the agent. The *parasmaipada* suffixes are used after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *anu* and *parā*; after *kṣip* when preceded by *abhi*, *ati*, and *pra*; after *muh* when preceded by *pari*; after *mūṣ* when preceded by *pari*; and after *ram* when preceded by *vi* and *ā*. The *parasmaipada* suffixes are optionally used after the root *ram* when it is intransitive; after the roots *budh*, *yudh*, *naś*, *jan*, *i*, *mud*, and *rus* when followed by a causative suffix (*ṇic*); and after roots having the meaning of swallowing (*niṃgaraṇa*) or moving (*calana*). The *parasmaipada* suffixes are used after roots that are intransitive and have a sentient being as their agent when followed by an affix denoting habitual action (*aṇau*); however, this does not apply to the roots *pā* (to drink), *dam*, *yama* with *āṅ*, *yā* with *āṅ*, *saṃ-pari-muh*, *ruc*, *mṛ*, *vad*, and *vas*. This applies to the root *yā* [in the aforementioned context].

[The following are the rules regarding the usage of prepositions and suffixes: *Prati*, *pari*, and *anu* are used with words expressing a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), a state of being so (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), a portion (*bhāga*), or repetition (*vīpsā*). *Abhi* is used in the sense of "except" (*abhāga*). *Prati* is used in the sense of a representative (*pratinidhi*) or in exchange (*pratidāna*). *Adhi* and *pari* are meaningless (*anarthaka*) when used as particles. *Su-* is used in the sense of praise (*pūjā*). *Ati-* is used in the sense of transgression (*atikramaṇa*) as well. *Api-* is used in the sense of a word-meaning (*padārtha*), possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), permission (*anvavasarga*), censure (*gardā*), or conjunction (*samuccaya*). *Adhi-* is used in the sense of lordship (*īśvara*). The word *yuvan* (young) is compounded with words denoting baldness (*khalati*), gray hair (*palita*), wrinkles (*vali*), and old age (*jaratī*); words having the same number of syllables (*kṛtyatulyākhyā*) are compounded with a word of lower caste (*ajāti*); a color-word (*varṇa*) is compounded with a word of higher caste (*varṇa*); the word *kumāra* (boy) is compounded with words such as *śramaṇa* (ascetic) and others; the word *catuṣpāt* (four-footed) is compounded with *garbhiṇī* (pregnant); the group beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* is a class of compounds; the suffix *ṇya* is optionally used after a word ending in *prāpta* or *āpanna*; words denoting time (*kālāḥ*) are compounded with a word denoting the thing measured (*parimāṇin*); the negative particle *nañ* is compounded with a word not ending in a primary suffix (*akṛtā*); the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is compounded with words such as *yājaka* (sacrificer) and others; there is no compounding in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*); the word *samartha* is compounded when it functions as another member of the compound (*anyapadārthe*); the words *siddha*, *śuṣka*, *san*, *mahat*, and numbers up to twelve are compounded; names of directions (*diṅnāmāni*) are compounded when expressing an intermediate direction (*antarāle*).

Thus ends the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter. In that [chapter], [the following rules apply]: 2.1.29: *tena* (by that), *idam* (this)—when these words are of the same form (*sarūpa*), [the compound is formed]; likewise for *pūrva*, *apara*, *adhara*, *uttara*, and a word denoting a part (*ekadeśin*), provided they have a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*). 2.1.30: *ardha* (half) is neuter [in such a compound]. 2.1.31: *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *caturtha*, and *turya* [are used similarly]. 2.1.32: *saha* (with) [is compounded] with that [word] when there is equality of connection (*tulyayoga*). 2.2.28: [The rule continues: *tena saha* (with that). When there is equality of connection, [the word *saha* is compounded with that word].

[The following are the relevant *sūtra*s: 2.1.72: *saṃkhyāvyayāsannādurādhika-saṃkhyāḥ saṃkhyeye* — Numerals, indeclinables (*avyaya*), words meaning "near" (*āsanna*), "distant" (*dūra*), "exceeding" (*adhika*), and numerals [are compounded] with a word denoting the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*). 2.2.24: *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadvyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena* — [A word ending in a case-affix is not compounded] with a word expressing a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*), a quality (*guṇa*), the sense of "satisfied" (*suhita*), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), or a word ending in the suffixes *-tavya* or *-anīya*, when they stand in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). By the rule of non-application (*abhāvānyayena*), the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is placed first; however, in the group beginning with *rājadanta* (e.g., *rājadantaḥ*), it is placed last. 2.2.3: *rājadantādiṣu param*. 2.2.4–2.2.14: [Rules concerning the order of members in a *dvandva* compound: 2.2.4: *dvandve ghi* — In a *dvandva*, that which ends in a vowel of the *ghi* class comes first. 2.2.5: *alpāctaram* — That which has fewer syllables comes first. 2.2.6: *abhyarhitam* — That which is more venerable comes first. 2.2.7: *bhrātuśca jyāyasaḥ* — And the elder brother's name comes first. 2.2.8: *dvandve ca* — [In a *dvandva* of names of deities, etc., the name of the deity Indra comes first. 2.2.9: *devatānām ca* — [And among the names of deities, the one with fewer syllables comes first. 2.2.10: *vā'ntara-pada-nimittaka-svara-bhinne* — [The above rules apply optionally when there is no difference in accent caused by internal word-formations. 2.2.25: *na dadhipayaādīni* — Words such as *dadhipayas* are exceptions. 2.2.26: *mātāpitarau ca* — The term *mātāpitarau* is an exception. 2.2.27: *pitāputrau ca* — The term *pitāputrau* is an exception. 2.2.11: *ajādyadantam* — In a *dvandva*, that which begins with a vowel other than *a* or ends in *a* comes first. 3.2.10: *tṛtīyā ca hoichandasi* — In the Veda, the third case-ending is also used [before the word *hi*]. 2.2.33: *ajādyadantam* — [In a *dvandva*,] that which begins with a vowel other than *a* or ends in *a* is placed first.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word ending in a shorter vowel precedes; likewise, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) precedes other words when it functions as an adjective. In the group beginning with *vāhitāgni*, the order may optionally be reversed. In a *karmadhāraya* compound, words beginning with *kaḍāra* (tawny) precede; furthermore, in the group beginning with *pūrvāpara*, *adharottara*, and *tṛtīyāprabhṛti*, eighteen such rules apply. Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter. When the object (*karman*) has not been already expressed by another grammatical means, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used. 2.1.39: When used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), words signifying "a little" (*stoka*), "few" (*alpa*), "with difficulty" (*kṛcchra*), as well as *kṛti*, *payas*, and *āyas*, [govern the genitive]. 2.3.34: With words signifying "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*), the genitive may optionally [be used] instead of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). 2.3.11: And [the genitive is used] with that [word] from which there is a substitute (*pratinidhi*) or an exchange (*pratidāna*). 2.3.35: After words signifying "far" or "near," the accusative (*dvitīyā*) may also [be used] in addition to the [genitive].

39. After a verb having the sense of "going," the second case (*dvitīyā*) and the fourth case (*caturthī*) are used for the object; and the seventh case (*saptamī*) is used for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), except when there is physical movement (*ceṣṭā*) on a path (*adhvan*). The fourth case is also used for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Furthermore, the fourth case is used for the object of a verb whose subordinate word (*upapada*) expresses the purpose of the action (*kriyārtha*). It is also used after a verbal noun (*bhāvavacana*) ending in *tum* (infinitive). It is used in connection with *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ*. Optionally, it is used for the object of the verb *man* when expressing disregard (*anādara*). It is used for the characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). Optionally, it is used for the object of the verb *samjñā*. This is the reading of the Sūtra.

In the sense of a cause (*hetau*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is optionally used when the agent or the object is not expressed (*akartṛkārake*), provided it does not end in a feminine suffix; the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also used in connection with the word *hetu*, and the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for pronouns (*sarvanāmnaḥ*). The fifth case is used for the ablative (*apādāne*). When joined with words other than *anyā*, *ārāt*, *itarat*, or directional terms (*dikśabda*), or with the words *ūrdhvam*, *uttara*, *pada*, *jā*, or *ahi*, the sixth case is used; likewise with words having the sense of the suffix *tasi* and with the word *enap*, the second case is used. With the words *pṛthak*, *vinā*, and *nānā*, the third case is optionally used. [Ablative] is also used to denote the time by which another action is marked (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*). The sixth case is also used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*). Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.26, 2.3.36, 2.3.12, 2.3.37, 2.3.13, 2.3.38.

79. *Ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.106): After a verbal root ending in long *ā*, when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), the suffix *gha* is applied; [examples are] *uddhana* ("striking upwards"), *atyāṃdhāna* ("excessive binding"), *apaghana* ("limb"). 80. *Ṇyāsaśrantho yuc* (Pāṇini 3.3.107): The suffix *yuc* is applied after roots ending in *ṇi*, as well as *ās* and *śranth*. 81. *Karaṇe'yovidruṣu* (Pāṇini 3.3.108): When the instrument (*karaṇa*) is expressed, provided that *ayas*, *vidruma*, or *drus* do not follow. 82. *Rogākhyāyāṃ ṇvul bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.108): The suffix *ṇvul* is frequently applied to express a name of a disease. 83. *Saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.109): [The suffix *ṇvul* is applied] when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed. 84. *Stambe ka ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.109): When *stamba* is the object, the suffix *ka* is also applied along with *ṇvul*. 85. *Vibhāṣākhyānaparipraśnayor-in-aṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.110): In the sense of "narrating" or "inquiring," the suffix *in* is optionally applied after a root ending in *aṅ*. 86. *Svapo nan upasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.91): After the root *svap* ("to sleep") preceded by a prefix, the suffix *nan* is applied. 87. *Ghoḥ kiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.92): After roots ending in *ghu*, the suffix *ki* is applied. 88. *Karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.93): The suffix *ktin* is applied in the feminine to denote the object (*karman*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). 89. *A0 pā0 sū0 3*: [This marks the end of the third chapter of the Aṣṭādhyāyī.]

12.1. The affixes *ha*, *ra*, and *ka* are used after the verb *udak* when it means "not water" (*anudaka*), provided that the negative particle *nañ* is present even if the interrogative pronoun *kim* is not; and the affix *gha* is also used after *khana*. The affix *khal* is used after the roots *bhū* and *kṛñ* when preceded by the particles *īṣat*, *duḥ*, and *su* in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*) or ease (*akṛcchra*), and it denotes both the agent and the object. In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the affix *yuc* is added to roots meaning "motion" (*gati*), and it is also seen after other roots. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used to express proximity to the present time (*vartamānasāmīpye*). The present tense (*laṭ*) is also used with the particles *kiṃ* and *kila* when they signify existence (*astyartha*). The potential mood (*liṅ*) is used after the particles *jātu* and *yadā*. The potential mood (*liṅ*) is also used after the particles *yat* and *yatra*. And [the potential mood is used] in connection with the word *gamyam*.

3.3.126: And [the conditional *liṅ* is used] when there is a sense of wonder (*citrikaraṇa*). 3.3.127: In the remaining cases, the present tense (*laṭ*) and the future tense (*luṭ*) are used. 3.3.128: After the particles *uta* and *api*, when they are semantically equivalent, the conditional (*liṅ*) is used. 3.3.129: After *kāmaṃ* when it expresses permission, provided that *kañcit* is not used. 3.3.130: When expressing a possibility (*sambhāvana*) with the word *alam*, the conditional (*liṅ*) is used if a verbal root follows. 3.3.131: In connection with the particle *dhik*, the conditional (*liṅ*) is optionally used after a verbal root when expressing a possibility. 3.3.132: [The conditional is used] when expressing a statement, provided that *yad* is not used. 3.3.133: The conditional (*liṅ*) is used to express cause and effect (*hetu-hetumat*). 3.3.134: After verbs meaning "to desire," the conditional (*liṅ*) and the imperative (*loṭ*) are used.

Pāṇini Sūtras 3.3.134–168: 134. When the agents are the same, the suffixes *tumun* (infinitive) and *liṅ* (optative) are used after roots meaning "to desire. 135. After roots meaning "to desire," the suffixes expressing the present tense may optionally be used in the sense of the present. 136. In the sense of hope (*āśaṃsā*), the suffix *vadvā* (the suffix *vā*, which is like the present tense) is used as if it were the past tense when there is a mention of speed; the suffix *lṛṭ* (future) is used in the sense of hope; and the suffix *liṅ* (optative) is used when there is a mention of hope. In the future tense, when there is no connection with the current day and no proximity of time, and when there is a specification of a limit (*maryādā*) within a division of time that does not include days and nights, the suffix *liṅ* is optionally used in the subsequent division of time. When there is a failure of the action (*kriyātipatti*), the suffix *laṅ* is used in place of the conditions for *liṅ*. [The suffix *liṅ* is also used] in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), and entreaty (*āmantraṇa*).

169. The suffix *tosun* is added after the roots *hu*, *dā*, *mi*, and *ja*, when necessity (*āvaśyaka*) or debt (*adhamarṇya*) is expressed. 170. The suffix *kasun* is added after the roots *sṛp* and *tṛd*. 171. When *alam* or *khalu* express prohibition, [the suffixes *tumun*, *ktvā*, and *kṛtya* are used]. 172. After a verb meaning "to be able" (*śaki*), the suffixes *tumun*, *ktvā*, *kṛtya*, and also *liṅ* are used; and *liṅ* and *loṭ* are used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). 173. The suffixes *tumun*, *ktvā*, and *kṛtya* are also used when expressing a name (*saṃjñā*). 174. According to the Northern Grammarians (*udīcām*), the suffix *tumun* is used after the root *māṅ* (*mā*) in the sense of exchange (*vyatīhāra*). 175. And also when there is connection with "before" (*parā*) or "after" (*avara*). 176. After the particle *māṅ*, the suffix *luṅ* is used. 177. When two actions have the same agent (*samānakartṛka*), the suffix *ktvā* is used for the action occurring at the earlier time (*pūrvakāla*). 178. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*). 179. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it expresses a reason (*hetu*) or purpose (*prayojana*). 180. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a sequence of actions (*anvādeśa*). 181. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a simultaneous action (*yugapad-kriyā*). 182. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a condition (*bhāva*). 183. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a quality (*guṇa*). 184. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a state (*avasthā*). 185. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a cause (*kāraṇa*). 186. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a result (*phala*). 187. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a purpose (*uddeśya*). 188. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a restriction (*niyama*). 189. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). 190. [The suffix *ktvā* is used] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) when it denotes a permission (*anujñā*). 191. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter [of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*], concerning the optional application of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *ūdh-* when denoting a masculine person. The third chapter is completed. The sūtras [of this section] are:

[The following are the rules from the Aṣṭādhyāyī: A feminine suffix (*ana*) added after words ending in *dāman* or *hāyana*, provided the penultimate vowel is elided, is optional; however, it is compulsory in technical names (*saṃjñā*) and Vedic literature (*chandas*). The suffix *ka* is applied after the words *kevala*, *māmaka*, *bhāgadheya*, *pāpa*, *āpa*, *para*, *samāna*, *ārya*, *kṛta*, *sumaṅgala*, *bheṣaja*, and *rātri* (provided the word ends in *rātri* when not followed by the dual endings *au* or *as*). The augment *nuk* is added after *antarvat* and *pativat*. The substitution of *un* for *pati* occurs when [the compound] refers to a sacrifice (*yajña-saṃyoga*). The substitution is optional when the word is preceded by another word; however, it is compulsory in the case of *sapatnī* and similar forms. The suffix *taddhita* is applied after *vṛṣākapi*, *aniku*, *sitakusīda*, and *āsuti*. The suffix *ka* is applied after words beginning with *vahat* in the Veda (*nityaṃ chandasi*). The suffix *ka* is applied after the root *bhū* when used in connection with a masculine (*puṃ-yogāt*) to denote a name (*ākhyāyām*). [End of Sūtra Text]

4.1.27–29: After words beginning with *gaura*, and after *jānapada*, *kuṇḍa*, *goṇa*, *sthala*, *bhājana*, *ānaka*, *kāla*, *nīla*, *kuśa*, *kāmuka*, and *kabara*, the feminine suffix *ūṅ* is applied [respectively] when they denote a profession, a vessel, that which is not artificial, a mixture, stoutness, color, clothing, an iron product, a desire for sexual intercourse, and a hair-style; furthermore, *ūṅ* is optionally applied after a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) ending in a vowel other than *u*. These are the rules.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the following words when they are preceded by the word *krīta* (bought) and form a *bahuvrīhi* compound denoting a name of a plant (*kāṇḍalpa*): *indu*, *varuṇa*, *bhava*, *śarva*, *rudra*, *mṛḍa*, *ahna*, *araṇya*, *yava*, *yavana*, *mātula*, and *ācārya*; provided that the final syllable of the first member of the compound is udātta. Furthermore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a word denoting a non-body-part (*asvāṅga*) which has an udātta on its final syllable, provided that the first member of the compound does not itself denote a body part (*svāṅga*). The suffix *ṅīṣ* is also applied after a word denoting a body part (*svāṅga*) that is an upasarjana (subordinate member of a compound), provided it does not end in a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyoga*) and has an udātta on its final syllable. The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a word denoting a body part ending in *nāsikā*, *udara*, *oṣṭha*, *jaṅghā*, *danta*, *karṇa*, or *śṛṅga*. [Note: The text fragment provided ends with "karṇaśṛṅgāca" (Pāṇini 4.1.55).]

35. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied] after words beginning with *kroḍa*, nor after those ending in *bahvac*, nor after those preceded by *sa-* or *nañ*, nor after *nakha* and *mukha* when they form a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Also, *dīrghajihvī* [is formed] in the Veda (*chandas*). 36. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied] after a word that has an udātta accent on its first syllable. 37–38. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after the word *manu* with the substitution of *au*; or, after a word ending in *varṇa* which has an anudātta accent on the final syllable and a *t* as its penultimate letter, the *t* is replaced by *n*. 39. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after the word *vāh* (in compounds). 40. [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a word preceded by a directional term (*dik*) as its prior member. 41. [The suffixes *sakhī* and *aśiśvī* are irregularly formed] in common usage (*bhāṣā*). [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after a genus-denoting word (*jāti*) that does not denote a female, provided it does not have *y* as its penultimate letter, and after words ending in *pāka*, *karṇa*, *parṇa*, *puṣpa*, *phala*, *mūla*, or *vālā*.

The suffixes *āvaṭya* and others are secondary derivatives (*taddhita*). The suffix *ti* is applied after [the word] *yuvan*. After [stems ending in] *aṇ* or *iñ*, provided they do not denote a descendant of Ṛṣis and have a heavy penultimate syllable, the suffix *pya* is applied in the sense of a *gotra*. After [stems denoting] a *gotra* that are parts of [the group beginning with] *kroḍi*, and after [the group beginning with] *daivayajñi*, *śaucivṛkṣi*, *sātyamugri*, and *kāṇṭheviddhi*, the suffix *pya* is optionally applied. Among words capable of being combined, the first case-ending is used optionally. Before the suffixes beginning with *divya*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Also after [the group beginning with] *aśvapati*, and after [stems] whose final member is *diti*, *aditi*, or *āditya*, the suffix *yañ* is applied in the sense of "his descendant. In the sense of a *gotra*, only one [descendant] is designated; in the sense of a *yuvan*, the suffix *iñ* is applied after [stems] other than those beginning with *stri*. The suffix *iñ* is also applied after [the group beginning with] *vāhla*. In the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, the suffix *akaṅ* is also applied in the sense of a *gotra*.

The suffix *añ* is applied after [patronymic] names derived from the word *mātṛ*, as well as from villages located in the north; the suffix *aṇ* is applied after [names] ending in a polysyllabic word with an acute accent on the final syllable, or those beginning with *masthottarapada* or *paladyādi*; the suffix *iñ* is applied after [names from] the *kaṇva* group and after patronymics (*gotra*) ending in *iñ*; the suffix *cha* is applied after [names] that are not *tryaca* (three-syllabled) and belong to the eastern regions or to *bharata*; the suffixes *ṭhak* and *chas* are applied after the word *bhavat*; the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *jiṭh* are optionally applied after [names from] the *kāśyādi* group; the suffix *ṭhañ* is optionally applied after villages of the *vāhīka* region, provided they are not among the *uśīnara* tribes; the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after place-names ending in *ora*; the suffix *huñ* is applied after [place-names] belonging to the easterners that have a long vowel (*vṛddhi*) or a *ya*-substitute as their penultimate letter; and the suffix *huñ* is also applied after [place-names] ending in *prastha*, *pura*, or *vaha*, or those having *ra* or *sa* as their penultimate letters. Aṣṭādhyāyī Sūtras 4.2.108–137.

The suffix *cha* is applied after [names of] non-desert regions (*apadāta*), after *sālva*, and after words ending in *go*, *yava*, and *vāyu* when followed by a secondary member (*uttarapada*). It is also applied after [words beginning with] *gaha* and others (Pāṇini 4.2.138). After [place names] of the Easterners (*prācām*) beginning with *kaṭa* (Pāṇini 4.2.139). After *rājan*, the suffix *ka* is also used (Pāṇini 4.2.140). After [names] containing a *vṛddhi*-vowel, excluding those ending in *eke*, *anta*, or having *kha* as a penultimate letter (Pāṇini 4.2.141). Also after [names of] countries (*janapada*) and their inhabitants (*tadvatya*), even if they do not contain a *vṛddhi*-vowel, provided they refer to the plural; likewise after [names] ending in *kaccha*, *anirgarta*, and *dhūma* and others (Pāṇini 4.2.129–137). After [names] ending in *pada* (Pāṇini 4.2.142). Also after *parvata* (Pāṇini 4.2.143). Optionally so, except when referring to a non-human being (Pāṇini 4.2.144).

[The suffix *aṇ* is applied after] *kṛkaṇaparṇa*, *bhāradvāja*, [and others] (Pāṇini 4.2.118–124). 65. The suffixes *vat* and *sa* are applied after the words *vatsa*, *ukṣan*, *aśva*, and *ṛṣabha* when expressing the sense of "truth" (*tattva*). 66. From the pronouns *kim*, *yat*, and *tat*, when used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) between two, the suffix *ḍatarac* is added; when used for selection among many, the suffix *ḍatamac* is added. Optionally, these suffixes may be added to case endings (*sup*) to form adjectives meaning "one of many. When the sense is "many," the suffix *bahuc* is added before the word. The suffix *ātīyar* is optionally added after a word ending in *ā*. The suffix *ka* is added after a word ending in *bhāga*. The suffix *kak* is added after indeclinables (*avyaya*), pronouns (*sarvanāman*), and nouns ending in *an*; in this case, the suffix *māk* is added before the word. 67. The suffix *kan* is added to form a name (*saṃjñā*). After the words *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā*, the suffix *upac* is added provided they do not end in *ku*.

45. After the word *kim*, when used in the sense of censure; after a word denoting "excessive grasping," "non-distress," or "censure"; after a word ending in the third case (instrumental), provided it does not denote the agent; and after a word connected with *hīyamāna* ("being deprived") or *pāpa* ("sinful"), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed. The suffix *ṣyañ* is added to a word denoting a disease to express its removal, provided it is joined with a verb of action (*kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*). The suffix *cvi* is added to a word ending in the third case to express the attainment of a state (*sampad*), provided it does not denote the agent. Furthermore, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final syllables of *aru*, *manas*, *cakṣus*, *cetas*, *rahas*, and *rajas*. The suffix *sāti* is optionally added in the same sense (*kārye*). The suffix *cvi* is also added to express pervasion (*abhividhi*), as well as with the root *sam-pad*. The suffix *tīn* is added to express a verbal activity (*vacane*). The suffix *nañ* is added after a *tatpuruṣa* compound beginning with *nañ* (negation). 5. 4. 45. (Continued) (Note: This is a summary of Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī, Sūtras 5.4.45–50.)

46. The substitution of *pathin* for *panthan* is optional after the words *deva*, *manuṣya*, *puruṣa*, *puru*, and *martya*, when followed by the second or seventh case endings, though not necessarily in all instances. After an imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) consisting of more than two syllables and ending in a vowel other than *iṭ*, the suffix *ḍāc* is added. The suffix *ḍāc* is also added after the verb *kṛ* (to do) when preceded by *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *śamba*, or *bīja* in the sense of ploughing. It is added after a numeral ending in *guṇa* (as a final member) and after the word *samaya* in the sense of "delaying" or "passing time. The suffix *ḍāc* is added after *sapatra* and *niṣpatra* in the sense of causing extreme pain; after *niṣkula* in the sense of exterminating; after *sukha* and its synonyms in the sense of compliance; after *duḥkha* and its synonyms in the sense of opposition; after *śūla* in the sense of cooking; after *satya* in the sense of an oath; and after *madrāt* in the sense of shaving. 47. [Continuation of the rule regarding the addition of *ḍāc*.]

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound where a numeral is the object of enumeration (*saṃkhyeya*), the suffix *ḍac* is applied [after the second member], with the exception of *abahu*. (Pāṇini 5.4.73) The suffix *ac* is applied after the words *ṛc*, *pura*, *abdhi*, and *dhur*, when they are preceded by *ān* and do not refer to a constellation (*nakṣatra*). 6.1.1: *ekāco dve prathamasya* — Of a monosyllabic root, the first [syllable] is reduplicated. 6.1.2: *ajāderdvitīyasya* — For a root beginning with a vowel, the second [syllable] is reduplicated. 6.1.3: *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ* — The letters *n*, *d*, and *r*, when they are the first members of a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), are not reduplicated. 6.1.4: *pūrvo 'bhyāsaḥ* — The preceding portion is called the "reduplicate" (*abhyāsa*). 6.1.5: *ubhe abhyastam* — Both [the reduplicate and the base] together are termed "repeated" (*abhyasta*). 6.1.6: *jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ* — The six roots beginning with *jakṣ* (to eat) are also designated as *abhyasta*. 6.1.7: *tujādīnāṃ dīrgho 'bhyāsasya liṭi* — In the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, there is lengthening of the reduplicate for roots beginning with *tuñj*. 6.1.8: *sanyoḥ* — [The rules regarding reduplication apply] before the suffixes *san* (desiderative) and *yaṅ* (intensive). 6.1.11: *vibhāṣā śveḥ* — Optionally, [the reduplication of *śvi* is treated as having a long vowel] before *san* and *yaṅ*. 6.1.13: *ṇau ca saṃcaṅoḥ* — And also before the causative suffix *ṇic*, and before *san* and *caṅ* (the aorist marker). 6.1.14: *hvaḥ samprasāraṇam* — There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the *h* of *hve* (to call) before *san* and *yaṅ*. 6.1.15: *abhyāsasyobhayeṣām* — Vocalization of the reduplicate occurs for both classes [of roots mentioned in 6.1.14]. 6.1.16: *liṭy abhyāsasyobhayeṣām* — Vocalization of the reduplicate occurs for both classes in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense. 6.1.17: *svapisyamivyeñāṃ yaṅi* — Vocalization of the reduplicate occurs for *svap*, *śvas*, and *vyeñ* in the *yaṅ* (intensive). 6.1.18: *na vaśaḥ* — Vocalization does not occur for the reduplicate of *vaś* (to desire). 6.1.19: There is no *samprasāraṇa* substitution for the vowel of the root *vay-* before the *liṭ* suffix; nor is there such substitution for the *v* of *vay-* optionally before a *kit* suffix, nor for the root *veñ*, nor for the roots *lī* (in the form *lyap*) and *jyā* (in the form *vyā*), except optionally after the prefix *pari*. A root-final vowel is not changed to *ai* (*ādeca*) in its original form (*upadeśe*) when followed by a suffix beginning with a non-śit (*aśiti*) letter. There is no *samprasāraṇa* for the root *vyo* before the *liṭ* suffix. For the roots *sphurati* and *sphulati*, the substitution of *v* for *u* occurs optionally. For the roots *krīḍ*, *jī*, etc., when used with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* occurs. For the root *sidh*, the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* occurs when it does not refer to the next world (*apāralaukike*). The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of *aṅka* occurs before a suffix beginning with a vowel. The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of a stem ending in *nṛ* occurs before a suffix beginning with a vowel. The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of a stem ending in *n* or *m* as a penultimate letter occurs before a case-ending beginning with a vowel. Before a case-ending that is a *sarvanāmasthāna* (excepting the vocative), the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of a stem ending in *ṣ* or preceded by *ṣ* occurs. In the Vedic language (*nigama*), the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of a stem ending in *s* or *m*, or of the word *mahat*, occurs before a *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending (excepting the vocative). The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of stems ending in *amṛta*, *vasu*, *vasana*, *sani*, *iṣṭa*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *kṣattṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, and *praśāstṛ* occurs before a *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending (excepting the vocative). The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of stems ending in *in*, *han*, *puṣan*, and *aryaman* occurs before the nominative singular suffix *su*. The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of a stem ending in *at* or *as* (provided they are not verbal roots) occurs before the nominative singular suffix *su*. The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of a nasalized stem occurs before the suffixes *kvip* and *jhal*. The substitution of *ū* for the final vowel of the root *tan* occurs before the suffix *san*. Optionally, the substitution of *ū* for the final vowel of the root *kam* occurs before the suffix *san*. The substitution of *ū* for the vowels *ch* and *ū* occurs before a suffix beginning with a nasal or when followed by a nasal.

38. After a preposition (*upasarga*), the augment *nuṭ* is added before the suffixes *kha*, *pat*, and *ṅī*; also after the words *ṣaṣ* and *catur*. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), it is added after *śrī* and *grāmaṇī*. At the end of a foot (*pādānta*) [of a verse], it is added after *go*. The augment *num* is added to a root ending in a nasal (*it*) when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel. The augment *śn* is added to the roots *muc* and others before a suffix beginning with a consonant (*jhal*). The augment *na* is added to the roots *radh* and *jabh* before a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ac*), except in the Perfect (*liṭ*). The augment *ra* is added to *rabh* before the suffix *aś* and in the Perfect (*liṭ*). The suffix *jāl* is added to *vyāyā*. The final *am* is elided in the *madhyama-puruṣa* plural (*majhū*) when followed by *dhvam*. In the *ātmanepada* forms, the *dhvam* is replaced by *dhvāt*, as in *yajadhvainam*. Also, the forms *tasya*, *tāv*, *tata*, *tanat*, and *thanā* are used for *idantomasi*. The suffix *gra* is added to *ktvā*, as in *iṣṭīnam*. Also, *snāvyādayaḥ* and *ājasera* [are formed].

43. *otaḥ śyani ksasyāci* (Pāṇini 6.1.91): In the case of the suffix *śyan*, the *o* of a root ending in *o* is elided before a suffix beginning with a vowel that follows a *kṛt* suffix marked with *k*. 44. *lugvā duhadihalihaguhāmātmanepade dantye śamāmaṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 6.4.91–96): - The suffix *śnu* is optionally elided (*luk*) after the roots *duh*, *diha*, *liha*, and *guh* when followed by an *ātmanepada* suffix beginning with a dental consonant. - In the *śyan* suffix, there is lengthening of the vowel for these eight roots: *śam*, *dam*, *tam*, *śram*, *bhram*, *kṣam*, *klam*, and *mad*. 46. *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.75): Before a suffix marked with *śit*, there is lengthening of the vowel for the roots *ṣṭhivu*, *klam*, and *cam*. 47. *kramaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.3.76): Before a *parasmaipada* suffix marked with *śit*, there is lengthening of the vowel for the root *kram*. 48. *iṣugamiyamāṃ chaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.77): Before a suffix marked with *śit*, the letter *ch* is substituted for the final letter of the roots *iṣ*, *gam*, and *yam*. 49. *pāghrādhmāsthāmnādāṇūdṛśyattisārttaśadasadāṃ pibajighradhamatiṣṭhamanayacchapaśyarchadhauśīyasīdāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.78): Before a suffix marked with *śit*, the following substitutions are made: - *pib* for *pā* (to drink) - *jighra* for *ghrā* (to smell) - *dham* for *dhmā* (to blow) - *tiṣṭha* for *sthā* (to stand) - *mana* for *mnā* (to study) - *yaccha* for *yama* (to restrain) - *paśya* for *dṛś* (to see) - *archa* for *ṛc* (to praise) - *dhau* for *dhāv* (to run) - *śīya* for *śad* (to fall) - *sīda* for *sad* (to sit). (These rules correspond to Pāṇini 7.3.78 through 7.3.84.)

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), after *ni*, *pra*, *pari*, and *upa*, the substitution of *ru* for *matup* and *vasu* occurs when followed by a word beginning with a vowel; and the substitution of *ud* for the final *u* of a word ending in *u* occurs before a root beginning with *stau* or *ṇi*, as well as in the case of *bhīroḥ* and *ānateḥ*. savarṇe* — After a *jhara* (consonants other than semivowels and nasals), there is the optional elision of a following *jhara* if they are homogeneous (*savarṇa*). 8.4.45: *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* — Before a nasal (*anunāsika*), a *yara* (all consonants except semivowels) may optionally become a nasal. 8.4.46: *aco rahābhyāṃ dve anaci ca* — After a vowel (*ac*) or after *ra* and *ha*, a consonant may be doubled, except when followed by another vowel (*anaci*). 8.4.47: *nādinyākrośe putrasya* — In the word *putra*, doubling occurs before a vowel in an abusive expression (*ākrośa*), provided it is not the name of one’s own mother (*nādini*). 8.4.48: *śaro 'ci* — Doubling occurs before a vowel after a sibilant (*śara*). 8.4.49: *a-bha-anta-prabhṛtiṣu śākaṭāyanasya* — According to Śākaṭāyana, doubling occurs in words beginning with *abha* (such as *abhyāsa*, *abhyutsāha*, etc. before a vowel. 8.4.50: *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade* — After *ra* or *ṣa*, *na* becomes *ṇa* within the same word (*samānapada*). 8.4.51: *aṭ-kupvāṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi* — The substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs even when there is intervention by vowels (*aṭ*), gutturals (*ku*), labials (*pu*), the letter *aṅ*, or the augment *num*. 8.4.52: *padavyavāye 'pi* — The substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs even when there is the intervention of a whole word (*pada*). 8.4.53: *kṣumnādiṣu ca* — The substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs in the group of words beginning with *kṣumnā*. 8.4.54: *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* — When *staḥ* (the letters *sa* and *ta*) come into contact with *śca* (sibilants and *ca*), they are replaced by *śca*. 8.4.55: *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* — When *ṣṭu* (the letters *ṣa* and *ta*) come into contact with *ṣṭu*, they are replaced by *ṣṭu*. 8.4.56: *na padāntāṭṭor anām* — The substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu* does not occur when *ṭu* follows a word-final (*padānta*) *ṣa* or *ta*, except in the case of the word *anām*. 8.4.57: *toḥ ṣi* — The substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṭu* does not occur when *ṭu* follows a word-final *ta* before a sibilant (*ṣi*). 8.4.58: *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* — Before a *jhaś* sound (voiced aspirates and nasals), *jhal* sounds (all consonants except semivowels and nasals) are replaced by *jaś* sounds (voiced unaspirated stops and nasals). 8.4.59: *abhyāse car ca* — In reduplicated syllables (*abhyāsa*), *car* sounds (voiceless unaspirated stops and sibilants) are also optionally replaced by *jaś* sounds. 8.4.60: *coḥ kuḥ* — In a reduplicated syllable, *cu* sounds (palatals) are replaced by *ku* sounds (gutturals). 8.4.61: *pumaḥ khayy am-parē* — After the word *pum*, the final *m* is replaced by *ru* before a *khaya* sound (voiceless consonants), provided that *am* follows. 8.4.62: *naś chavy apraśān* — After the word *praśān*, the final *n* is replaced by *ru* before a *chavi* sound (voiceless consonants), except when *praśān* itself ends in *n*. 8.4.63: *dīrghāt padāntād vā* — After a long vowel at the end of a word (*padānta*), the final *n* may optionally be replaced by *ru* before a *chavi* sound. 8.4.64: *nṝn pe* — After the word *nṝn*, the final *n* is optionally replaced by *ru* before the word *pa*. 8.4.65: *sarvatra śākalyasya* — According to Śākalya, the final *n* of a word is always replaced by *ru* before a *chavi* sound. 8.4.66: *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ* — A low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) following a high-pitched vowel (*udātta*) becomes circumflex (*svarita*). 8.4.67: *nodāttasvaritodayam agārgyakāśyapagālavānām* — According to Gārgya, Kāśyapa, and Gālava, a vowel that is followed by a high-pitched (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel does not become circumflex. 8.4.68: *svaritāt saṃhitāyām anudāttānām* — In continuous speech (*saṃhitā*), after a circumflex vowel, all following low-pitched vowels become circumflex. 8.4.69: *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ* — When a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) replaces both a high-pitched and a low-pitched vowel, the resulting single substitute is high-pitched (*udātta*). 8.4.70: *svarito vānudātte padādau* — Or, if the following vowel begins a word and is low-pitched (*anudātta*), the single substitute may optionally be circumflex (*svarita*). 8.4.71: *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* — The final *n* of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is elided. 8.4.72: *na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ* — The final *n* is not elided in the genitive singular ending *-ṅasi* or in the vocative singular (*saṃbuddhi*). 8.4.73: *ṅṇoḥ kuk ṭuk śari* — Before a sibilant (*śari*), the augment *kuk* is added after a word ending in *ṅ* or *ṇ*. 8.4.74: *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ* — Before the genitive singular suffix *si*, the augment *dhuṭ* is added after a word ending in *ḍ*. 8.4.75: *traṃ ca* — The augment *traṃ* is also added after a word ending in *ḍ* before *si*. 8.4.76: *dhuṭ-prakarane rātsasya* — In this section concerning augments, the suffix *sa* is elided after *rā*.

Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.119: *mato bahuco'najirādīnām* || [The suffix *matup* is added after a polysyllabic word ending in *mat*,] except for the *ajirādi* group. The *ajirādi* group is as follows: 33. *ajira*, *khadira*, *pulina*, *haṃsaka* (or *haṃsa*), *kāraṇḍa* (or *kāraṇḍava*), *cakravāka*. (3) 133. And [the words] beginning with *anuśatika* [have udātta on the final syllable]. 7.3.20.

*anuśatika*, *anuhoḍa*, *anusaṃvaraṇa* (*anusaṃcaraṇa*), *anusaṃvatsara*, *aṅgāraveṇu*, *asihatya*, *asyahatya*, *asyaheti*, *vadhyoga*, *puṣkarasat*, *anuharat*, *kurukata*, *kurupañcāla*, *udakaśuddha*, *ihaloka*, *paraloka*, *sarvaloka*, *sarvapuruṣa*, *sarvabhūmi*, *prayoga*, *parastri*, *rājapuruṣāyatri*, *mūtranaḍa*. This is the group beginning with *anuśatika*. It is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); therefore, [the following are also included]: *abhigama*, *adhibhūta*, *adhideva*, *caturvidyā*.

And so forth. || 4 || 47. *The addition of kṣipakā and others [to the list of words that do not take the feminine suffix ī] is prescribed.* || 7.3.45 || *kṣipakā, dhruvakā, carakā, setakā, karakā, caṭakā, avakā, halakā, alakā, kanyakā, dhruvakā, eḍakā.* Thus ends the group beginning with kṣipakā. It is an open-ended class (ākṛtigaṇa). || 5 || 104. *And [the substitution of short i for the final vowel of the penultimate syllable occurs] in the case of nyaṅku and others.* || 7.3.53 ||

nyaṅku, maddha, bhṛgu, dūrepāka, phalepāka, kṣaṇepāka, dūrepāka, phalepāka, dūrepāku, phalepāku, takra (tatra), vakra (cakra), vyatiṣaṅga, anuṣaṅga, avasarga, upasarga, vapāka, māṃsapāka (māsapāka), mūlapāka, kapotapāka, ulūkapāka; and in the sense of a technical name (saṃjñāyām), meghanidāghāvapāṣāḥ and nyagrodhaviruta. Thus ends the *nyakkādi* group. 7. It should be stated that [the rule] applies to *kaṇa* and the others as well. 4.3.131. *kaṇādīnāṃ ca*. (And for *kaṇa* and the others.)

*kaṇa*, *raṇa*, *bhaṇa*, *śraṇa*, *lupa*, *heṭha*, *hāyi*, *vāṇi*, *loṭi*, *lopi*. Thus ends the *kaṇādi* group. [End of] the Eighth Chapter. 210. *tiṅo gotrādīni kutsanābhīkṣṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.27). The words *gotra*, *bruva*, *pravacana*, *mahasana*, *prakathana*, *pratyayana*, *mapañca*, *māya*, *nyāya*, *pracakṣaṇa*, *vicakṣaṇa*, *avacakṣaṇa*, *svādhyāya*, *bhūyiṣṭha*, and *vāna* follow a finite verb (*tiṅ*) when contempt (*kutsana*) or repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*) is expressed. 1.213. *Pūjanāt pūjita-manudāttaṃ kāṣṭhādibhyaḥ* (8.1.67). [The suffix] *matup* is anudātta after words beginning with *kāṣṭha* when they denote that which is honored (*pūjita*). The *kāṣṭhādi* group is as follows: *kāṣṭha*, *dāruṇa*, *amatāputra*, *veśa*, *anājñāta*, *anujñāta*, *aputra*, *ayuta*, *adbhuta*, *anukta*, *bhṛśa*, *ghora*, *sukha*, *parama*, *su*, *ati*. End of the *kāṣṭhādi* group. 2.163. *Mādupadhāyāś ca mator vo 'yavādibhyaḥ* (8.2.9). [The substitution of] *v* for the *m* of *matup* occurs after a word ending in *m* or *u*, or having *m* or *u* as its penultimate letter, provided it is not one of the *yava-ādi* group.

*yava*, *dalbhi*, *ūrmi* (or *urmi*), *bhūmi*, *kṛmi*, *kruñcā*, *vaśā*, *drākṣā*, *prākṣā*, *dhani*, *vraji*, *dhvani*, *niji*, *siji*, *sañji*, *harit*, *kakut*, *marut*, *garut*, *ikṣu*, *dru*, *madhu*. Thus ends the *yavādi* group; it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). **Gaṇapāṭha:** 14. *Aharādīnām patyādiṣūpasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 8.2.70): An addition [to the rule] regarding *ahar* and others before words beginning with *pati*. 1. *ahar*, *gīr*, *dhūr*. Thus ends the *aharādi* group. 2. *pati*, *gaṇa*, *putra*. Thus ends the *patyādi* group.

12. *Kaskādiṣu ca* 8.3.48. [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] also in the group beginning with *kaska*. Examples: *kaskaḥ*, *kautaskutaḥ*, *bhrātuṣputraḥ*, *śunaskarṇaḥ*, *sadyaskālaḥ*, *sadyaskīḥ*, *sādyaskaḥ*, *kāṃskān*, *sarpiṣkuṇḍikā*, *dhanuṣkapālam*, *vahippalam* (*varhippalam*), *yajuṣpātram*, *ayaskāntaḥ*, *tamaskāṇḍaḥ*, *ayaskāṇḍaḥ*, *medaspiṇḍaḥ*, *bhāskaraḥ*, *ahaskaraḥ*. [End of section.]

*suṣāmā*, *niḥṣāmā*, *duḥṣāmā*, *suṣedhaḥ*, *niṣedhaḥ*, *niḥṣedhaḥ*, *duḥṣedhaḥ*, *suṣaṃdhiḥ*, *niḥṣaṃdhiḥ*, *duḥṣaṃdhiḥ*, *suṣṭhu*, *duṣṭu*; *gauripakthaḥ* when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*); *pratiṣṇikā*, *jalāṣāham* (or *jalāṣāḍam*), *nauṣecanam*, *dundubhiṣevaṇam* (or *dundubhiṣecaṇam*); [the word] *eti* [is included] in a proper name after [a word ending in] *agāt*; or [after a word] denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Examples: *hariṣeṇaḥ*, *rohiṇīṣeṇaḥ*. Thus ends the *suṣāmādi* group; it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class).

133. *Na* [is substituted for the final vowel] before *rapara*, *sṛpi*, *sṛji*, *spṛh*, and words beginning with *savana*. *sabane sabane* (at every pressing), *sūte sūte* (at every birth), *some some* (at every Soma sacrifice), *savanamukhe savanamukhe* (at every commencement of a pressing), *kiṃsaṃ kiṃsam* (what kind of [Soma]?, what kind of [Soma]?), *anusavanam anusavanam* (at each pressing), *gosaniṃ gosanim* (the winner of cows, the winner of cows), *aśvasanim aśvasanim* (the winner of horses, the winner of horses). Alternative reading: *savana-savane*, *savanamukha-savanamukhe*, *anusavana-anusavanam*. In the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*): *bṛhaspatisavaḥ* (the Bṛhaspati-sacrifice), *śakunisavanam* (the bird-sacrifice).

*sute sute*, *saṃvatsare saṃvatsare*, *visaṃ visam*, *kisaṃ kisam*, *musalaṃ musalam*, *gosanim aśvasanim*. *girinitamba*, *cakranadī*, *cakranitamba*, *tūryamāna*, *māṣona*, *ārgayana*. Thus ends the section beginning with *girinadī* (10). **8.4.39**: *kṣumnādiṣu ca* (and in the case of words in the *kṣumnādi* group). *kṣubhra*, *nṛnamana*, *nandin*, *nandana*, *nagara*. These words as final members [of a compound] cause the substitution of *ṇatva* when they denote a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *harinandī*, *harinandanaḥ*, *girinagaram*. They also cause the substitution of *ṇatva* when preceded by *nṛ* or *tiryañc*. Examples: *narīnṛtyate*, *nartana*, *gahana*, *nandana*, *niveśa*, *nivāsa*, *agni*, *anūpa*.

These function as final members [of compounds]. *parinartanam*, *parigahanam*, *parinandanam*, *śaraniveśaḥ*, *śaranivāsaḥ*, *śarātriḥ*, *darbhānūpaḥ*; and the state of being a pupil (*ācāryadaṇḍatvam*). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). An alternative reading: *bhuja*, *tṛpnu*, *nunamana*, *nara*, *nagara*, *nandana*, *yanṛtī*, *girinadī*, *gṛhagamana*, *niveśa*, *nivāsa*, *ani*, *anūpa*, *ācāryabhogīna*, *caturhāyana*. Words beginning with *irikā* form compounds with *vana* as the final member when used as proper names (*saṃjñāyām*).

*irikā*, *timira*, *samīra*, *kubera*, *hari*, *karmāra*. Thus ends the *kṣumnādi* group (11). Thus concludes the *Gaṇapāṭha* composed by the venerable sage Pāṇini. (2) The *Dhātupāṭha*: *ṭīkṛ* 105, *tikṛ* 106, *tīkṛ* 107, *raṣi* 108, *laghi*—these have the meaning of "motion.
